newsitem.title: FRANCE: French election could hang on palm-tree vote.
newsitem.headline: French election could hang on palm-tree vote.

text.p: The final result of France's two-round general election, in which European unity issues loom large, may depend on voters who have never set foot in Europe -- the residents of French overseas territories.

Projections released early on Monday, after Sunday's first-round vote, showed competition for the 555 National Assembly seats for metropolitan France would be extremely close with perhaps only a handful of seats separating the ruling centre-right and the opposition.
The nation votes a second time next Sunday in hundreds of districts where no candidate achieved an overall majority of votes in the first round.

Leading commentators said it was now quite possible that the overall result would hang on the 22 electoral districts in French overseas possessions strung around the globe, from the Caribbean to the Indian Ocean to the South Seas.

"Everything that has been said so far has dealt with metropolitan France," said political scientist Alain Duhamel. "Now, let us not forget the DOM-TOMs (Overseas Departments and Territories) because they could make the ultimate choice."
The possibility of such a scenario has existed for decades but has not yet seriously been put to the test.
Of the 22 overseas seats, the centre-right held 12 in the outgoing assembly, the left six and independents, who voted either way according to the issue, the final four.
French Polynesia, with two seats, voted last week, the only area under French rule to do so. Both of its seats went to the centre-right.
- New Caledonia in the south Pacific, two seats
- St. Pierre et Miquelon off Canada's Atlantic coast, one seat.
- Mayotte island in the Indian ocean, one seat.
- Wallis and Futuna in the Pacific, one seat.
- French Guiana, on the northeast coast of South America and wracked by demonstrations in recent weeks, two seats.
- Guadeloupe island in the West Indies, four seats.
- Martinique, also in the West Indies, four seats.
- Reunion island in the Indian ocean, five seats.
